newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin seeks backing for reform from Russia media.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin seeks backing for reform from Russia media.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, preparing Russia for a new-look government and a painful leap forward in economic reform, turned to the powerful media on Friday for support.

"Today your word may turn out to be extremely important, if not decisive," Yeltsin, who is in the process of making a radical government reshuffle with a pledge to revitalise reforms, said in an appeal to journalists in a radio address.

The 66-year-old Kremlin leader announced he was back as the nation's leader after months of illness in a keynote speech on March 6, saying Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government was unable to tackle a deep social and economic crisis.

He acknowledged in his speech to parliament that more then half of all Russians were unhappy with the state of affairs, but said improvements could be reached only by completing the reforms which he said had stalled during his absence.

"Immediately after that (speech), the first steps were made to implement it, first of all by making changes in the government," Yeltsin said in his Friday address, referring to the naming of reformer Anatoly Chubais as Chernomyrdin's number two.
"I am talking about more energetic and consistent continuation of reforms than before."
The liberals who spearheaded the first phase of reforms five years ago became widely unpopular, partly becasue they failed to explain clearly to people why the changes were needed.
Russians are now suspicious about any reform plans, fearing they mean further drops in living standards with no clear benefits.
The new cabinet will face growing public discontent over long delays in wage and pension payments, and the expected closure of many enterprises paralysed by non-payments.
Government handouts for education, health care, housing and municipal services may have to be cut.
Yeltsin's liberal aides acknowledge that such objectives cannot be reached in an impoverished country without serious social strains. Media support could be vital in the process.

The president's election campaign last year was bolstered by favourable coverage in the liberal media and particularly by the main television channels. He turned to the media again on Friday, urging them to back the new government.

"(Your publications) can soothe people, give them some common sense, strengthen their will or incite more hostility, scepticism," he said. "I realise there is a great temptation to pour out your woes, whip the authorities for unprofessional decisions.
"But we are living in one country, in a common home," he added. "One can help clean it, throw away garbage, but one may also keep shouting: "It is so dirty, so ugly here."
He added: "The freedom of press is one of the main gains of Russia which in not questioned even by its foes."

"We see how much society needs and has got used to freedom of speech, how it sees it as habitual and routine," he added. "A turn back to the age of humiliating lies, a show of unanimity is impossible."
